core.title: Structural optimization of drug molecules with incrementally trained language models
core.abstract: Abstract Automating structural optimization of drug molecules for on-target potency by machine learning is an open challenge in chemistry. Here, we capitalize on the ability of chemical language models (CLMs) to learn from sequential data and design new molecules with desired properties. We establish a training strategy mimicking the learning trajectory of a drug discovery program. Incremental CLM fine-tuning with increasingly potent template molecules from a given structure-activity relationship (SAR) series successfully biases the model to design highly active analogues. Prospective application of this technique to ligand development enables the data-driven design of molecules exceeding known representatives of given bioactive chemotypes in potency without external scoring. Our results reveal an ability of CLMs to capture SAR patterns and long-range dependencies, and to exploit SAR knowledge in designing analogues with improved on-target activity de novo corroborating their applicability to structural optimization of drug molecules.

core.title: Agentic4PDM: Host-Governed Evidence Admissibility for Industrial Fault Diagnosis
core.abstract: We study industrial fault diagnosis as a classification task that assigns sensor time-series windows to predefined health states or fault types. Scarce labels and changing operating conditions make repeated training of specialized classifiers costly. Yet structures such as periodicity, trends, and transients can remain diagnostically informative and be examined through reusable analytical tools. LLM agents can select and interpret these tools, but fixed rules or training-derived guidance may not resolve each signal's ambiguity, while unconstrained interpretation may overstate weak or conflicting results. We introduce Agentic4PDM, a framework that separates adaptive investigation from control over evidence use. LLM agents compare each signal with labeled references from every candidate class, identify unresolved distinctions, and propose follow-up measurements. A deterministic software controller, called the host, enforces contract-checked gated adjudication (CCGA): it checks requests, requires commitment to a complete tool batch before results are observed, and assigns evidence roles based on tool checks against labeled references. These roles distinguish corroborative support from advisory information. The Judge Agent proposes a diagnosis, while the controller checks protocol compliance and records the investigation. Agentic4PDM supports training-free diagnosis using pretrained representations and labeled references without task-specific diagnostic models, and a standard setting that additionally investigates trained-model predictions. Experiments on selected bearing and motor diagnosis challenges and an unfiltered industrial test set supplied by our customer show gains in aggregate macro F1 over the evaluated diagnostic and agentic baselines. Ablations further support the value of the governed workflow.

core.title: Transfer learning framework for fatigue life prediction of additively manufactured parts
core.abstract: Additive manufacturing has the potential to make things more efficient because of its ability to build customizable products quickly and with fewer resources required. The issue that additive manufacturing faces is the inferior performance relative to conventionally manufactured parts in the long run, thus hindering their adoption in mission-critical applications. The main cause of this inferior performance in as-built parts is surface roughness, which can not be avoided due to process physics. The deep valleys in the surface act as stress concentration areas that become crack initiation sites, thus leading to part failure. The scarcity of fatigue testing data compounds this problem, as fatigue tests are expensive in terms of time and cost. Transfer learning is a machine learning technique used to handle the problem of smaller datasets for training by leveraging the model learned for a related task and using it for the target task. This work aims to use the transfer learning technique and fatigue test data to build a framework that learns from the surface roughness data and makes predictions about fatigue life. This framework can potentially solve the data scarcity problem in studying the fatigue behavior of additively manufactured parts, thus facilitating their adoption in a wide spectrum of applications with confidence.

core.title: PROTEAN: Beyond De Novo Generation - Can LLM Agents Perform Text-Guided Protein Structure Editing?
core.abstract: Generative AI has achieved remarkable success in de novo protein design, yet protein engineering typically begins with existing, characterized proteins. The primary demand is targeted local editing, e.g., engineering a specific region to optimize affinity, alter immunogenicity, or improve stability, while strictly preserving core catalytic motifs and overall scaffold integrity. However, no standardized framework currently exists for carrying out and evaluating such edits. In current generative-design workflows, researchers often need to manually specify complex low-level parameters and rely on repetitive, trial-and-error sampling and evaluation across generative backends to search for viable conformations. While large language models (LLMs) offer an intuitive interface to express these goals using natural language, prevailing structure-generation models cannot directly interpret high-level human instructions. To bridge this gap, we introduce PROTEAN, a standardized benchmark for text-guided protein structural editing. PROTEAN comprises 380 sub-tasks spanning six intervention families and evaluates a two-stage pipeline in which an LLM translates natural-language goals into backend-specific geometric constraints and a generative model remodels the protein backbone. A two-tier evaluation separates geometric compliance, including target attainment and off-target scope fidelity, from biophysical realizability assessed by inverse folding and refolding consistency. Across five frontier LLMs paired with three backends, strict end-to-end biophysical success starts at just 7.0%. Ablation studies show that LLM constraint compilation is already highly accurate, whereas the main bottlenecks are backend-specific scope leakage and refolding failure. PROTEAN provides an open testbed for developing autonomous, multi-backend macromolecular design agents.

extended.abstract: This chapter explores the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) in fatigue analysis and reliability assessment. It highlights how AI/ML techniques can enhance various aspects of fatigue research, including data analysis, life prediction, crack detection, and surrogate modeling. Unlike many engineering applications, fatigue reliability is characterized by limited data availability and high uncertainty, posing unique challenges for data-driven methods. To address this, the chapter introduces physics-guided and uncertainty-aware ML frameworks that integrate domain knowledge with data-driven models. Neural networks (NNs), including deep learning architectures, are discussed for tasks such as S-N curve prediction, crack growth modeling, and the modeling of manufacturing processes and microstructures. The chapter also emphasizes the importance of incorporating uncertainty into AI models to ensure robust and reliable predictions. Hybrid approaches that combine physics-based models with ML are presented as a promising direction for future research. The chapter concludes by presenting a neural optimization approach for advanced fatigue design using AI/ML. Overall, this chapter provides a forward-looking perspective on how AI/ML can transform fatigue reliability analysis in the era of data-driven engineering.

extended.title: How the Classical Baseline Shapes Machine-Learning Speed Claims in Topology Optimization
extended.abstract: Topology optimization places material so that a structure resists deformation under given loads. Machine-learning methods often report large speed-ups over classical, non-learned optimization, but a slow classical code or a less stiff learned design can exaggerate them. We re-ran released code for eight methods on one workstation and studied two in depth: Optimize Any Topology (OAT), a diffusion model that generates designs, and a graph-based neural optimizer. Speeding up only the classical code's finite-element solver cut these two methods' speed-ups by up to 20-fold. We then timed the classical code until its design was at least as stiff as the learned one; for OAT, we read this point off the completed runs. Published timings imply a 134x speed-up for OAT on a 256 x 256 grid; our matched single-design comparisons gave 1.5x to 3.5x. At matched stiffness, the graph-based optimizer was slower than the classical code in all six two-dimensional problems. Of the six other methods, two kept their advantage, one shrank, one reversed and two were not comparable. In an exploratory audit of published claims, language models judged that 8 of 28 speed comparisons in randomly sampled, openly accessible articles lacked evidence of equal design quality; our own review counted 11, so the count depends on who judges. We provide a comparison procedure and a minimum report: classical code, hardware, design quality, what each timing includes, and data-generation and training costs.

extended.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
extended.abstract: The rapid convergence of the Internet of Things (IoT), Blockchain, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and Machine Learning (ML) is fundamentally reshaping the landscape of modern digital infrastructure. While each of these paradigms has individually driven massive technological leaps, their true transformative power lies in their synergy. IoT acts as the sensory network collecting real-world data, Blockchain provides an immutable layer of security and decentralized trust, and AI/ML serves as the cognitive brain processing this information to enable real-time, autonomous decision-making. Advanced Computing Technologies: IoT, Blockchain, AI, and Machine Learning offers a comprehensive exploration of these core pillars, bridging foundational theory with real-world system design, architectural frameworks, and deployment strategies.The text begins by establishing core computing paradigms, historical evolution, hardware architectures, distributed systems, and the socio-economic drivers of Industry 4.0. It then transitions into the mechanics of intelligent connected systems, detailing sensor networks, embedded devices, communication protocols from MQTT to 5G and 6G, and the evolution toward the Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT). From there, the book examines cryptographic primitives, consensus mechanisms, smart contract development, and decentralized security models within Blockchain and Distributed Ledger Technologies. Turning to the intelligence layer, it thoroughly explores classical machine learning, deep neural networks, transformer architectures, computer vision, Generative AI, Explainable AI, and privacy-preserving Federated Learning. Finally, the narrative synthesizes these pillars into unified architectures, showcasing cutting-edge developments such as digital twins, zero-knowledge machine learning (zkML), agentic AI, quantum paradigms, and sustainable computing.Tailored for undergraduate and graduate students, academic researchers, solution architects, and technology leaders, this book balances rigorous conceptual foundations with practical case studies spanning smart grids, autonomous transport, precision agriculture, and digital healthcare. By examining both individual components and integrated ecosystems, this work provides a complete roadmap for designing scalable, secure, and resilient cyber-physical systems. Whether utilized as a university textbook or an industry reference guide, this volume aims to empower readers to navigate, innovate, and lead in an increasingly interconnected and intelligent digital world.

extended.title: Beyond global drug-likeness: The FamDLike framework as a target family-specific drug-likeness score.
extended.abstract: Drug-likeness is a central metric which is used to evaluate the physicochemical profile of small molecules either as a filter for virtual screening or, more recently, as a reward function in generative design tasks. Established scores such as QED are widely adopted for these purposes, although the ligands of different therapeutic target families occupy different regions of physicochemical space. Applying a single global drug-likeness criterion can therefore systematically reward some target classes while penalising others, narrowing the chemical space considered druglike in a way that may not reflect the actual requirements for a given project. In this work, we propose a target family specific drug-likeness approach, the FamDLike framework, designed to distinguish target families more accurately than existing metrics and to explore family specific druglike regions of chemical space. This framework combines three complementary modelling paradigms: desirability functions, generalized additive models and tree-based machine learning models that span the interpretability-flexibility spectrum. The three components can also be used independently, depending on whether interpretability or predictive flexibility is prioritized. The abilities of the proposed method have been tested on real-world use cases in computational medicinal chemistry: an independent set from DrugBank, library screening of Enamine and KLIFS compounds, and de novo molecule generation via REINVENT4. The proposed approach therefore provides a more discriminative, interpretable and target-aware complement to existing drug-likeness scores, suitable for ranking in early discovery pipelines and as a reward function for generative chemistry. Furthermore, a user-friendly web portal (https://huggingface.co/spaces/kochgroup/FamDLike) is available to obtain drug-likeness profiles of molecules.

papers.title: Structural optimization of drug molecules with incrementally trained language models
papers.abstract: Abstract Automating structural optimization of drug molecules for on-target potency by machine learning is an open challenge in chemistry. Here, we capitalize on the ability of chemical language models (CLMs) to learn from sequential data and design new molecules with desired properties. We establish a training strategy mimicking the learning trajectory of a drug discovery program. Incremental CLM fine-tuning with increasingly potent template molecules from a given structure-activity relationship (SAR) series successfully biases the model to design highly active analogues. Prospective application of this technique to ligand development enables the data-driven design of molecules exceeding known representatives of given bioactive chemotypes in potency without external scoring. Our results reveal an ability of CLMs to capture SAR patterns and long-range dependencies, and to exploit SAR knowledge in designing analogues with improved on-target activity de novo corroborating their applicability to structural optimization of drug molecules.

papers.title: Agentic4PDM: Host-Governed Evidence Admissibility for Industrial Fault Diagnosis
papers.abstract: We study industrial fault diagnosis as a classification task that assigns sensor time-series windows to predefined health states or fault types. Scarce labels and changing operating conditions make repeated training of specialized classifiers costly. Yet structures such as periodicity, trends, and transients can remain diagnostically informative and be examined through reusable analytical tools. LLM agents can select and interpret these tools, but fixed rules or training-derived guidance may not resolve each signal's ambiguity, while unconstrained interpretation may overstate weak or conflicting results. We introduce Agentic4PDM, a framework that separates adaptive investigation from control over evidence use. LLM agents compare each signal with labeled references from every candidate class, identify unresolved distinctions, and propose follow-up measurements. A deterministic software controller, called the host, enforces contract-checked gated adjudication (CCGA): it checks requests, requires commitment to a complete tool batch before results are observed, and assigns evidence roles based on tool checks against labeled references. These roles distinguish corroborative support from advisory information. The Judge Agent proposes a diagnosis, while the controller checks protocol compliance and records the investigation. Agentic4PDM supports training-free diagnosis using pretrained representations and labeled references without task-specific diagnostic models, and a standard setting that additionally investigates trained-model predictions. Experiments on selected bearing and motor diagnosis challenges and an unfiltered industrial test set supplied by our customer show gains in aggregate macro F1 over the evaluated diagnostic and agentic baselines. papers.title: Transfer learning framework for fatigue life prediction of additively manufactured parts
papers.abstract: Additive manufacturing has the potential to make things more efficient because of its ability to build customizable products quickly and with fewer resources required. The issue that additive manufacturing faces is the inferior performance relative to conventionally manufactured parts in the long run, thus hindering their adoption in mission-critical applications. The main cause of this inferior performance in as-built parts is surface roughness, which can not be avoided due to process physics. The deep valleys in the surface act as stress concentration areas that become crack initiation sites, thus leading to part failure. The scarcity of fatigue testing data compounds this problem, as fatigue tests are expensive in terms of time and cost. Transfer learning is a machine learning technique used to handle the problem of smaller datasets for training by leveraging the model learned for a related task and using it for the target task. This work aims to use the transfer learning technique and fatigue test data to build a framework that learns from the surface roughness data and makes predictions about fatigue life. This framework can potentially solve the data scarcity problem in studying the fatigue behavior of additively manufactured parts, thus facilitating their adoption in a wide spectrum of applications with confidence.

papers.title: PROTEAN: Beyond De Novo Generation - Can LLM Agents Perform Text-Guided Protein Structure Editing?
papers.abstract: Generative AI has achieved remarkable success in de novo protein design, yet protein engineering typically begins with existing, characterized proteins. The primary demand is targeted local editing, e.g., engineering a specific region to optimize affinity, alter immunogenicity, or improve stability, while strictly preserving core catalytic motifs and overall scaffold integrity. However, no standardized framework currently exists for carrying out and evaluating such edits. In current generative-design workflows, researchers often need to manually specify complex low-level parameters and rely on repetitive, trial-and-error sampling and evaluation across generative backends to search for viable conformations. While large language models (LLMs) offer an intuitive interface to express these goals using natural language, prevailing structure-generation models cannot directly interpret high-level human instructions. To bridge this gap, we introduce PROTEAN, a standardized benchmark for text-guided protein structural editing. PROTEAN comprises 380 sub-tasks spanning six intervention families and evaluates a two-stage pipeline in which an LLM translates natural-language goals into backend-specific geometric constraints and a generative model remodels the protein backbone. A two-tier evaluation separates geometric compliance, including target attainment and off-target scope fidelity, from biophysical realizability assessed by inverse folding and refolding consistency. Across five frontier LLMs paired with three backends, strict end-to-end biophysical success starts at just 7.0%. Ablation studies show that LLM constraint compilation is already highly accurate, whereas the main bottlenecks are backend-specific scope leakage and refolding failure. PROTEAN provides an open testbed for developing autonomous, multi-backend macromolecular design agents.

papers.title: Fatigue Analysis with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
papers.abstract: This chapter explores the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) in fatigue analysis and reliability assessment. It highlights how AI/ML techniques can enhance various aspects of fatigue research, including data analysis, life prediction, crack detection, and surrogate modeling. Unlike many engineering applications, fatigue reliability is characterized by limited data availability and high uncertainty, posing unique challenges for data-driven methods. To address this, the chapter introduces physics-guided and uncertainty-aware ML frameworks that integrate domain knowledge with data-driven models. Neural networks (NNs), including deep learning architectures, are discussed for tasks such as S-N curve prediction, crack growth modeling, and the modeling of manufacturing processes and microstructures. The chapter also emphasizes the importance of incorporating uncertainty into AI models to ensure robust and reliable predictions. Hybrid approaches that combine physics-based models with ML are presented as a promising direction for future research. The chapter concludes by presenting a neural optimization approach for advanced fatigue design using AI/ML. Overall, this chapter provides a forward-looking perspective on how AI/ML can transform fatigue reliability analysis in the era of data-driven engineering.

papers.title: How the Classical Baseline Shapes Machine-Learning Speed Claims in Topology Optimization
papers.abstract: Topology optimization places material so that a structure resists deformation under given loads. Machine-learning methods often report large speed-ups over classical, non-learned optimization, but a slow classical code or a less stiff learned design can exaggerate them. We re-ran released code for eight methods on one workstation and studied two in depth: Optimize Any Topology (OAT), a diffusion model that generates designs, and a graph-based neural optimizer. Speeding up only the classical code's finite-element solver cut these two methods' speed-ups by up to 20-fold. We then timed the classical code until its design was at least as stiff as the learned one; for OAT, we read this point off the completed runs. Published timings imply a 134x speed-up for OAT on a 256 x 256 grid; our matched single-design comparisons gave 1.5x to 3.5x. At matched stiffness, the graph-based optimizer was slower than the classical code in all six two-dimensional problems. Of the six other methods, two kept their advantage, one shrank, one reversed and two were not comparable. In an exploratory audit of published claims, language models judged that 8 of 28 speed comparisons in randomly sampled, openly accessible articles lacked evidence of equal design quality; our own review counted 11, so the count depends on who judges. We provide a comparison procedure and a minimum report: classical code, hardware, design quality, what each timing includes, and data-generation and training costs.

papers.title: ADVANCED COMPUTING TECHNOLOGIES: IoT,BLOCKCHAIN, AI, AND MACHINE LEARNING
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The rapid convergence of the Internet of Things (IoT), Blockchain, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and Machine Learning (ML) is fundamentally reshaping the landscape of modern digital infrastructure. While each of these paradigms has individually driven massive technological leaps, their true transformative power lies in their synergy. IoT acts as the sensory network collecting real-world data, Blockchain provides an immutable layer of security and decentralized trust, and AI/ML serves as the cognitive brain processing this information to enable real-time, autonomous decision-making. Advanced Computing Technologies: IoT, Blockchain, AI, and Machine Learning offers a comprehensive exploration of these core pillars, bridging foundational theory with real-world system design, architectural frameworks, and deployment strategies.The text begins by establishing core computing paradigms, historical evolution, hardware architectures, distributed systems, and the socio-economic drivers of Industry 4.0. It then transitions into the mechanics of intelligent connected systems, detailing sensor networks, embedded devices, communication protocols from MQTT to 5G and 6G, and the evolution toward the Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT). From there, the book examines cryptographic primitives, consensus mechanisms, smart contract development, and decentralized security models within Blockchain and Distributed Ledger Technologies. Turning to the intelligence layer, it thoroughly explores classical machine learning, deep neural networks, transformer architectures, computer vision, Generative AI, Explainable AI, and privacy-preserving Federated Learning. Finally, the narrative synthesizes these pillars into unified architectures, showcasing cutting-edge developments such as digital twins, zero-knowledge machine learning (zkML), agentic AI, quantum paradigms, and sustainable computing.Tailored for undergraduate and graduate students, academic researchers, solution architects, and technology leaders, this book balances rigorous conceptual foundations with practical case studies spanning smart grids, autonomous transport, precision agriculture, and digital healthcare. By examining both individual components and integrated ecosystems, this work provides a complete roadmap for designing scalable, secure, and resilient cyber-physical systems. Whether utilized as a university textbook or an industry reference guide, this volume aims to empower readers to navigate, innovate, and lead in an increasingly interconnected and intelligent digital world.

papers.title: Beyond global drug-likeness: The FamDLike framework as a target family-specific drug-likeness score.
papers.abstract: Drug-likeness is a central metric which is used to evaluate the physicochemical profile of small molecules either as a filter for virtual screening or, more recently, as a reward function in generative design tasks. Established scores such as QED are widely adopted for these purposes, although the ligands of different therapeutic target families occupy different regions of physicochemical space. Applying a single global drug-likeness criterion can therefore systematically reward some target classes while penalising others, narrowing the chemical space considered druglike in a way that may not reflect the actual requirements for a given project. In this work, we propose a target family specific drug-likeness approach, the FamDLike framework, designed to distinguish target families more accurately than existing metrics and to explore family specific druglike regions of chemical space. This framework combines three complementary modelling paradigms: desirability functions, generalized additive models and tree-based machine learning models that span the interpretability-flexibility spectrum. The three components can also be used independently, depending on whether interpretability or predictive flexibility is prioritized. The abilities of the proposed method have been tested on real-world use cases in computational medicinal chemistry: an independent set from DrugBank, library screening of Enamine and KLIFS compounds, and de novo molecule generation via REINVENT4. The proposed approach therefore provides a more discriminative, interpretable and target-aware complement to existing drug-likeness scores, suitable for ranking in early discovery pipelines and as a reward function for generative chemistry. Furthermore, a user-friendly web portal (https://huggingface.co/spaces/kochgroup/FamDLike) is available to obtain drug-likeness profiles of molecules.
